title: Fleurons
subtitle: Small crescent-shaped puff pastry decorations for garnishing pies and sauced dishes
excerpt: Fleurons are small crescent or leaf shapes cut from puff pastry trimmings and baked until puffed and golden. They have been used as a garnish in classical French cooking since the eighteenth century: arranged around the edge of a vol-au-vent, set against a fish pie, or floating in a cream sauce. They take five minutes to cut and eight minutes to bake.
sourceNotes: Fleurons (from the French word for ornament or flower) are documented in classical French cookery from Escoffier onwards. They are made from puff pastry trimmings, cutting them into crescent shapes using two overlapping cuts with a round cutter. Standard patisserie and garde-manger references describe their use as garnishes for sauced dishes, fish preparations, and celebration pies.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked fleurons on a tray until firm, then transfer to a bag. Bake from frozen at 200 degrees Celsius for 12 to 14 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make as many as needed from puff pastry trimmings. Use trimmings immediately or chill before baking.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Baked fleurons keep in an airtight tin for 2 days. Refresh in a 180 degrees Celsius oven for 3 minutes before serving.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. Very hot oven is essential for puff pastry to rise properly.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small crescent or leaf-shaped pieces of puff pastry baked until golden and puffed. Used as a classical French garnish for sauced fish, pies, and vol-au-vents. Cut from a rolled sheet using two overlapping circles from a round cutter: one cut gives a disc, the second cut into the disc gives the crescent.

content.text: Fleurons turn puff pastry trimmings into a finished component. The

shape comes from making two overlapping circular cuts: the overlap gives you a crescent from the centre and two smaller side pieces. Chill before baking so the butter is cold and the layers separate cleanly in the oven.

items.prepNote: bought all-butter, or puff pastry trimmings from another recipe
beaten with a pinch of salt for egg wash

content.text: Roll the puff pastry on a lightly floured surface to about 4 mm thickness. Use a round cutter (5 to 6 cm diameter). Make a full circle cut, then place the cutter overlapping the first circle by about one-third and cut again. The crescent shape comes from the overlapping second cut.
Arrange the crescents on a lined baking tray without touching. Brush lightly with egg wash; avoid letting egg run down the cut sides, as this seals the layers and prevents the pastry from rising.
Chill for 15 minutes. Brush with a second coat of egg wash just before baking. Score a light curved line across each crescent with the back of a knife for decoration, if desired.

Bake at 200 degrees Celsius for 8 to 12 minutes until puffed and deep golden. Watch closely after 8 minutes; the high sugar content in all-butter pastry means they can catch quickly. Cool on a wire rack. Fleurons should have visible layers and a hollow sound when tapped.

Puff pastry trimmings should not be re-stacked and re-rolled like shortcrust; stacking scrambles the layers. Instead, lay the trimmings flat and slightly overlapping in the same direction, then roll gently once in the direction of the layers. The fleurons will not rise as high as those from fresh pastry but will still have distinct layers.
